court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 45 OHA 158 — IN RE WATTS
text:
IN THE MATTER OF LINDA WATTS
DIR-2012-0032 Decided March 7, 2013
Appeal from a determination made by a Board of Survey, Oregon State Office,
Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Portland, Oregon, finding employee, Linda
Watts, financially liable for the loss of government equipment due to negligence.
Report of Survey No. ORBRS11-002.
Reversed.
1. Property Board of Survey: Negligence
For the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals to affirm a Board of Survey’s
determination of employee liability in simple negligence, the
record must show that the loss of property was the result of the
employee’s failure to exercise the degree of care in which a
prudent person would exercise under like circumstances.
APPEARANCES: Linda Watts, Hines, Oregon, pro se.
OPINION BY CHAIRMAN JOSUHA N. EPSTEIN
Introduction
Appellant, Linda Watts, a BLM employee in the Burns District Office, Hines,
Oregon, has appealed the January 31, 2012, decision of the Reviewing Authority
affirming the determination of the Board of Survey, BLM, Oregon State Office,
Portland, Oregon (Board), which found Appellant negligent and financially liable for
loss of Government property—a Trimble Juno SB Handheld Global Positioning
System, Serial No. 41000093100339 (Property No. L0522487 Asset 84667) (property
or GPS). The loss occurred on June 14, 2010, when Appellant was performing a
weed survey in a fuel treatment unit. The Board assessed $250.00 in damages, and
Appellant received notice of the decision via a January 31, 2012, memorandum from
Jason Moss, Property Utilization Specialist, National Operations Center, Denver,
Colorado.
The Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) received the appeal on February
27, 2012, and the appeal is therefore timely. 43 C.F.R. § 4.701. OHA has assigned

DIR-2012-0032
the above-captioned docket number to the matter and obtained BLM’s official file. Id.
at § 4.702. Therefore, the matter is ready for disposition.
The Board of Survey Decision
Appellant provided an initial statement on a “Missing/Damaged Property”
form:
On June 14th, I was using the [GPS] for navigation and weed
survey in . . . a fuels unit . . . . As there was no place to secure the unit
to the ATV and navigate drive [sic] the ATV at the same time, I had unit
on the seat. I last used unit on NE side of unit to see where I was
within the unit and then started looking for a way to the road East of
unit, when I got to the road, noticed unit was gone.
Appellant’s “Missing/Damaged Property” statement, dated January 24, 2011.
Appellant supplemented that initial statement by informing the Board that her
office had started “working on a way to attach GPS units to the ATV’s [sic].”
Appellant’s Letter to Board of Survey Chairperson, May 11, 2011.
The Board made the following Findings and Determinations:
On 06/14/2010 Ms. Watts was conducting weed surveys on an
ATV in a fuel treatment unit. In the course of her work she was using a
GPS unit for navigation and site locations. As there was no means to
attach the GPS unit to the ATV she set it down on the seat as she
negotiated her way out of the unit. When she reached the road she
noticed it was missing. A number of attempts were made to recover the
unit.
Employees have a responsibility to safeguard Government
property from damage and loss. Ms. Watts failed to exercise due
diligence by not securing the unit to her persons [sic] as there was no
means to attach it to the ATV. Each individual is normally and
regularly responsible for using whatever means available to secure
small, valuable too [sic] their person in order to avoid loss.
The board finds that there was SIMPLE NEGLIGENCE on the
part of Ms. Watts. This will result in and assessment of financial
responsibility of $250.00 for the [loss of the Government property].
Findings and Determinations, ORBRS11-0002.

The Board received concurrence from the Deputy Regional Solicitor in
the Department of the Interior’s Pacific Northwest Region. That official found
that Appellant “failed to safeguard her equipment,” and that such conduct
“resulted in the loss of the equipment.” Memorandum from Deputy Regional
Solicitor, dated Oct. 25, 2011.
Argument on Appeal
Appellant has provided the following statement to this Board:
On June 14, 2010, I was using the [GPS] unit for navigation and
weed survey in . . . a fuels unit . . . . As there was no place to secure
the unit to the [ATV], navigate and drive the ATV at the same time, I
placed the unit on the seat between my legs. I last used the unit on the
northeast side of the fuels unit to check my location, and then started
looking for a way through the juniper, brush, and boulders to a road . .
. . When I arrived at the road the GPS unit was gone. Caryn Meinicke
(another Bureau of Land Management employee) and I back-tracked
my path and did an extensive search from the road back through the
fuels unit. Do [sic] to the dense Shrub cover, the color and small size
of the GPS unit, it was not located. The GPS unit had a black protective
“otter box” of which covered most of the bright yellow on the unit and
blended well with the surrounding rocks and shade of the brush.
On June 18, 2010, I went back with the SWAT crew and
searched for the GPS unit again.
In September, 2010, Caryn went back and did another search for
the GPS unit.
Tim Newkirk, Burns District Forester, asked his cutters to keep
an eye out for the GPS unit, when they were . . . in the fuels unit.
The Determinations stated that the GPS unit should have been
attached to my person; however I had no way to attach the GPS to
either the ATV or my person and still use it to navigate through the
fuels unit.
Appeal, dated February 23, 2012.
Appellant has also provided the following supporting statement from the
Burns District Office Manager:
45 OHA 160

DIR-2012-0032
On June 14, 2010 Linda Watts, an employee on our district, was
performing routine field work and inadvertently lost the Global
Positioning System (GPS) unit she was using to navigate and collect
data. Despite many attempts to locate the unit, it was not found.
After reviewing the situation with the employee and her field
supervisor, I determined that the Bureau of Land Management Burns
District had not provided adequate means to secure the GPS unit.
Following that incident, the weed program purchased brackets designed
to secure the GPS units while using them to navigate in the field.
While I regret the loss of the equipment, I do not believe it was
negligence on the part of the employee but rather inadequate means to
secure the equipment which was to blame.
I believe the employee had secured the GPS unit as best she
could under the circumstances . . . . I am prepared to accept the loss of
the equipment as an unfortunate learning experience which has already
led to greatly improved methods for securing our GPS property.
Memorandum from District Office Manager Brendan Cain, dated Feb. 24,
2012.
Review of the Survey Decision
[1] Without question, the Government has suffered a property loss. The
particular issue here is whether the Board properly concluded that the GPS was lost
due to simple negligence by the Appellant. 410 DM 114-60.808-1(b)(2). Simple
negligence involves “an act or omission of the employee in which he/she failed to
exercise the degree of care, precaution, attention, and vigilance which a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances.” Id. Regardless of whether an
accident or loss occurs, this Office may find an employee liable only if the record
“convincingly demonstrate[s] . . . that the employee acted in an imprudent manner.”
410 DM 114-60.808-1(a). As this Office has stated, a Board’s negligence finding
must be based on more than cursory findings and conclusions. In re Victoria
Hartman, 42 OHA 96, 99 (2011).
Here, we cannot affirm the Board’s simple negligence finding. The Board
determined that Appellant had a duty to use available means to secure small and
valuable property such as the GPS. Board of Survey Findings and Determinations,
OBRS11-0002. It failed to identify, however, any means that actually were available
to her. As a result, there is no basis for concluding that Appellant’s conduct
constituted a failure to meet the duty that the Board found applicable.
45 OHA 161

DIR-2012-0032
Similarly, the Board also relied on a BLM memorandum stating that employees
working in the field must “inventory equipment frequently.” Burns District Office
Memorandum, dated Oct. 1, 2010; see also Memorandum from Deputy Regional
Solicitor. Appellant stated that she checked for the property upon exiting a shrub-
covered area and reaching a road. Appeal at 1. The Board did not establish the
frequency with which Appellant should have inventory-checked the GPS and, as a
result, identified no basis for concluding that Appellant checked too late, or less
frequently than she ought to have. See In re Kevin C. O’Reilly, 31 OHA 16, 23-24
(2005) (negligence finding reversed where employee lost keys in backcountry despite
reasonable attempts to meet requirement that he secure them to his person at all
times). Nevertheless, even if there was a basis to conclude that Appellant did not
make sufficient efforts to safeguard the GPS unit while working in the field, the
Board cited no evidence that the property was lost as a result of her effort, or lack
thereof. See In re Scott L. Meneely, 39 OHA 287, 292 (2009) (negligence finding
reversed due to a Board of Survey’s “mere speculation” that a failure to meet a duty
resulted in the property loss).
We hereby reverse the Board’s finding of simple negligence and grant the
appeal. Appellant is not financially liable for the loss of the Trimble Juno SB GPS
unit. 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(3).
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(3), 410 DM 60.808-7.
